title: Why Christians will not call God Zeus
source_text: Καὶ τάχα οὐκ ἐλάττων ὁ κίνδυνος τῷ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ θεοῦ ἢ τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ ἐφ᾿ ἃ μὴ χρὴ κατάγοντι, ἤπερ τῷ τὰ κατά τινα ἀπόῤῥητον λόγον ὀνόματα ἐναλλάσσοντι καὶ τὰ μὲν κατὰ τῶν ἐλαττόνων φέροντι ἐπὶ τὰ κρείττονα τὰ δὲ κατὰ τῶν κρειττόνων ἐπὶ τὰ ἥττονα. καὶ οὐ λέγω ὅτι τῷ Διῒ εὐθέως συνεξακούεται ὁ Κρόνου καὶ Ῥέας υἱὸς καὶ Ἥρας ἀνὴρ καὶ Ποσειδῶνος ἀδελφὸς καὶ Ἀθηνᾶς καὶ Ἀρτέμιδος πατὴρ καὶ ὁ τῇ θυγατρὶ Περσεφόνῃ μιγεὶς, ἢ τῷ Ἀπόλλωνι συνεξακούεται ὁ Λητοῦς καὶ Διὸς υἱὸς καὶ Ἀρτέμιδος ἀδελφὸς καὶ Ἑρμοῦ ὁμοπάτριος ἀδελφὸς, καὶ ὅσα ἄλλα φέρουσιν οἱ σοφοὶ Κέλσου τῶν δογμάτων πατέρες καὶ ἀρχαῖοι θεολόγοι Ἑλλήνων. τίς γὰρ ἡ ἀποκλήρωσις, κυριολεκτεῖσθαι μὲν τὸν Δία οὐχὶ δὲ καὶ τὸν πατέρα μὲν αὐτοῦ εἶναι Κρόνον μητέρα δὲ Ῥέαν; τὸ δ᾿ ὅμοιον ποιητέον καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν ἄλλων ὀνομαζομένων θεῶν. τοῦτο δὲ τὸ ἔγκλημα οὐδαμῶς ἅπτεται τῶν κατά τινα ἀπόῤῥητον λόγον τὸ Σαβαὼθ τασσόντων ἐπὶ τοῦ θεοῦ ἢ τὸ Ἀδωναῒ ἤ τι τῶν λοιπῶν ὀνομάτων. ὅταν δὲ τὰ περὶ ὀνομάτων τις δύνηται τὰ ἐν ἀποῤῥήτοις φιλοσοφεῖν, πολλὰ ἂν εὕροι καὶ περὶ τῆς ἐπικλήσεως τῶν ἀγγέλων τοῦ θεοῦ· ὧν ὁ μέν τις Μιχαὴλ ἕτερος δὲ Γαβριὴλ καὶ ἄλλος Ῥαφαὴλ καλεῖται. φερωνύμως τοῖς πράγμασιν, ἃ διακονοῦνται κατὰ βούλημα τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν ὅλων ἐν τῷ παντί. τῆς δ᾿ ὁμοίας ἔχεται περὶ ὀνομάτων φιλοσοφίας καὶ ὁ ἡμέτερος Ἰησοῦς, οὗ τὸ ὄνομα μυρίους ἤδη ἐναργῶς ἑώραται δαίμονας ἐξελάσαν ψυχῶν καὶ σωμάτων, ἐνεργῆσαν εἰς ἐκείνους ἀφ᾿ ὧν ἀπηλάθησαν. ἔτι δ᾿ εἰς τὸν περὶ ὀνομάτων τόπον λεκτέον ὅτι οἱ περὶ τὴν χρῆσιν τῶν ἐπῳδῶν δεινοὶ ἱστοροῦσιν, ὅτι τὴν αὐτὴν ἐπῳδὴν εἰπόντα μὲν τῇ οἰκείᾳ διαλέκτῳ ἔστιν ἐνεργῆσαι ὅπερ ἐπαγγέλλεται ἡ ἐπῳδή· μεταλαβόντα δὲ εἰς ἄλλην οἱανδηποτοῦν φωνὴν ἔστιν ἰδεῖν ἄτονον καὶ οὐδὲν δυναμένην. οὕτως οὐ τὰ σημαινόμενα κατὰ τῶν πραγμάτων ἀλλ᾿ αἱ τῶν φωνῶν ποιότητες καὶ ἰδιότητες ἔχουσί τι δυνατὸν ἐν αὐταῖς πρὸς τάδε τινὰ ἢ τάδε. οὕτω δ᾿ ἀπολογησόμεθα διὰ τῶν τοιούτων καὶ περὶ τοῦ μέχρι θανάτου ἀγωνίζεσθαι Χριστιανοὺς, ἵνα μὴ τὸν Δία θεὸν ἀναγορεύσωσι μηδ᾿ ἄλλῃ διαλέκτῳ αὐτὸν ὀνομάσωσιν. ἢ γὰρ ἀορίστως ὁμολογοῦσι τὸ κοινὸν ὄνομα τὸ θεὸς ἢ καὶ μετὰ προσθήκης τῆς·“ ὁ δημιουργὸς τῶν ὅλων, ὁ ποιητὴς οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς, ὁ καταπέμψας τῷ γένει τῶν ἀνθρώπων τούσδε τινὰς τοὺς σοφούς“· ὡς τῷ ὀνόματι ἐφαρμοζόμενον τὸ θεὸς ὄνομα δύναμίν τινα παρὰ ἀνθρώποις ἐπιτελεῖ. πολλὰ δ᾿ ἂν καὶ ἄλλα λέγοιτο εἰς τὸν περὶ ὀνομάτων τόπον πρὸς τοὺς οἰομένους δεῖν ἀδιαφορεῖν περὶ τῆς χρήσεως αὐτῶν. καὶ εἴπερ θαυμάζεται Πλάτων εἰπὼν ἐν Φιλήβῳ· „τὸ δ᾿ ἐμὸν δέος, ὦ Πρώταρχε. περὶ τὰ ὀνόματα τῶν θεῶν οὐκ ὀλίγον.“ ἐπεὶ Φίληβος θεὸν τὴν ἡδονὴν εἶπεν ὁ προσδιαλεγόμενος τῷ Σωκράτει· πῶς οὐ μᾶλλον τῆς εὐλαβείας ἀποδεξόμεθα Χριστιανοὺς, μηδὲν τῶν ἐν ταῖς μυθοποιΐαις παραλαμβανομένων ὀνομάτων προσάπτοντας τῷ τοῦ παντὸς δημιουργῷ; ἀλλὰ γὰρ τούτων ἐπὶ τοῦ παρόντος ἅλις.
pass_a_gloss: And perhaps the danger (κίνδυνος) is not less for the one bringing down (κατάγω) the name of God or the name of the good onto what it must not (ἐφ᾿ ἃ μὴ χρή), than for the one exchanging (ἐναλλάσσω) the names according to some secret account (ἀπόρρητος λόγος) and carrying those [said] of the lesser (ἐλάττονα) onto the better (κρείττονα), and those of the better onto the inferior (ἥττονα). And I do not say (οὐ λέγω, paralipsis) that with Zeus there is at once heard along (συνεξακούω) the son of Cronus and Rhea, and husband (ἀνήρ) of Hera, and brother of Poseidon, and father of Athena and Artemis, and the one who had intercourse (μίγνυμι, aor. pass. ptc.) with his daughter Persephone; or with Apollo there is heard along the son of Leto and Zeus, and brother of Artemis, and brother by the same father (ὁμοπάτριος) of Hermes, and whatever else the wise fathers of Celsus's doctrines (δόγματα) and ancient theologians (θεολόγοι) of the Greeks bring. For what [is] the arbitrary allotment (ἀποκλήρωσις): Zeus to be named in the proper sense (κυριολεκτέω), but not also his father to be Cronus and mother Rhea? The like must be done (ποιητέον) also with the other named gods. This charge (ἔγκλημα) in no way touches (ἅπτομαι) those who according to some secret account place (τάσσω) Sabaoth upon God, or Adonai, or any of the remaining names. Whenever one can philosophise (φιλοσοφέω) the things about names that are in secret [doctrines] (ἐν ἀπορρήτοις), he would find much also about the naming/invocation (ἐπίκλησις) of the angels (ἄγγελοι) of God, of whom one is called Michael, another Gabriel, and another Raphael, aptly named (φερωνύμως) for the tasks (πράγματα) which they serve (διακονέω) according to the will (βούλημα) of the God of the universe (ὁ θεὸς τῶν ὅλων) in the all (τὸ πᾶν). To the like philosophy about names holds also our Jesus, whose name has already been clearly (ἐναργῶς) seen (ὁράω, pf. pass.) having driven out (ἐξελαύνω) countless (μυρίοι) demons from souls and bodies, having worked (ἐνεργέω) upon those from whom they were driven off (ἀπελαύνω). Further for the topic (τόπος) about names it must be said that those skilled about the use of incantations (ἐπῳδαί) relate (ἱστορέω) that [one] saying the same incantation in its own (οἰκεία) dialect can effect (ἐνεργέω) what the incantation professes (ἐπαγγέλλομαι); but changing it (μεταλαμβάνω) into any other speech (φωνή) whatever, one can see it slack (ἄτονος) and able nothing. Thus not the things signified (τὰ σημαινόμενα) about the things, but the qualities (ποιότητες) and properties (ἰδιότητες) of the sounds have something powerful (δυνατόν) in themselves toward these or those. Thus we will defend (ἀπολογέομαι) through such [arguments] also concerning Christians' contending (ἀγωνίζομαι) unto death so as not to proclaim (ἀναγορεύω) Zeus God nor name him in another dialect. For either they confess (ὁμολογέω) indefinitely (ἀορίστως) the common name 'God', or also with the addition (προσθήκη): 'the craftsman of the universe, the maker (ποιητής) of heaven and earth, the one who sent down (καταπέμπω) to the race (γένος) of men these certain wise men (τούσδε τινὰς τοὺς σοφούς)'; as the name 'God', fitted (ἐφαρμόζω) to the name, accomplishes (ἐπιτελέω) some power among men. Many other things also might be said for the topic about names against those thinking one must be indifferent (ἀδιαφορέω) about their use (χρῆσις). And if Plato is admired (θαυμάζω) saying in the Philebus: 'My fear (δέος), Protarchus, about the names of the gods [is] not small', since Philebus, the one conversing with Socrates, called pleasure (ἡδονή) a god(dess); how shall we not rather accept/approve (ἀποδέχομαι) for their caution (εὐλάβεια) Christians, attaching (προσάπτω) none of the names taken up in the myth-makings (μυθοποιΐαι) to the craftsman of the all (ὁ τοῦ παντὸς δημιουργός)? But of these, enough (ἅλις) for the present.
pass_b_english: And perhaps the danger is no less for one who brings the name of God, or the name of the good, down to things it should not be given to, than for one who interchanges the names that belong to a secret teaching, applying those of lesser things to greater, and those of greater things to lesser. I pass over the fact that with the name Zeus one at once hears along with it the son of Cronus and Rhea, the husband of Hera, the brother of Poseidon, the father of Athena and Artemis, and the one who lay with his daughter Persephone; or that with Apollo one hears the son of Leto and Zeus, the brother of Artemis, and the brother of Hermes on his father's side; and whatever else is told by those wise fathers of Celsus's doctrines, the ancient theologians of the Greeks. For what arbitrary choice lets the name Zeus be taken in its proper sense, but not also the statement that his father is Cronus and his mother Rhea? The same must be done with the other gods who are named.

But this charge in no way touches those who, according to a certain secret teaching, apply Sabaoth, or Adonai, or any of the other names to God. Whoever can philosophise about names in their hidden meanings would also find much about the names by which the angels of God are called: one of them is called Michael (Daniel 10:13), another Gabriel (Luke 1:19), and another Raphael (Tobit 12:15), names that fit the tasks they perform in the universe by the will of the God of all. Our Jesus too belongs to a like philosophy of names: his name has already been plainly seen to drive countless demons out of souls and bodies, taking effect upon those from whom they were driven out.

Further, on the topic of names it must be said that those skilled in the use of incantations report that the same incantation, spoken in its own language, can accomplish what the incantation promises; but translated into any other tongue whatever, it can be seen to be feeble and powerless. So it is not the meanings that stand for things, but the qualities and peculiarities of the sounds, that have a certain power in themselves for this purpose or that.

By such arguments we shall also defend the Christians for struggling even to death so as not to proclaim Zeus as God, nor to name him in another language. For they confess either the common name "God" without further definition, or with the addition, "the Maker of all, the Creator of heaven and earth (Psalm 146:6), who sent down to the human race these particular wise men"; for the name "God", joined to this designation, works a certain power among men. Much else could be said on the topic of names against those who think one need not care how they are used. And if Plato is admired for saying in the Philebus, "My fear, Protarchus, about the names of the gods is no small one" (Plato, Philebus 12c), because Philebus, who was conversing with Socrates, had called pleasure a goddess, how shall we not rather approve the reverent caution of the Christians, who attach to the Maker of the universe none of the names taken up in the mythologies? But enough of this for the present.

choices.choice: οὐ λέγω ὅτι ('I do not say that') is read as paralipsis, since Origen goes on to press the point; rendered 'I pass over the fact that'. ἀποκλήρωσις = arbitrary selection; the sentence is condensed in the Greek ('Zeus named properly, but not his father Cronus and mother Rhea') and the second κυριολεκτεῖσθαι is supplied. The angel names are inline-cited at a place each is named in Scripture (Michael, Daniel 10:13; Gabriel, Luke 1:19, also Daniel 8:16; Raphael, Tobit 12:15, deuterocanonical); Origen is not quoting a verse. The exorcisms by Jesus's name are presented as present experience (ἤδη ... ἑώραται); possible background in Mark 16:17 and Acts 16:18, left uncited. The Christian formula 'the Maker of heaven and earth' echoes Psalm 146:6 (LXX Psalm 145:6, τὸν ποιήσαντα τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν; also Genesis 14:19, 22); it is a confessional phrase rather than a quotation, cited as a clear allusion. τούσδε τινὰς τοὺς σοφούς ('these particular wise men') presumably means Moses and the prophets; left as in the Greek. ὡς τῷ ὀνόματι ἐφαρμοζόμενον ...: τῷ ὀνόματι taken as the descriptive designation just given; the clause is compressed and the sense uncertain. Philebus 12c: Origen paraphrases Plato (who has τὸ δ᾿ ἐμὸν δέος ... περὶ τὰ τῶν θεῶν ὀνόματα οὐκ ἔστι κατ᾿ ἄνθρωπον); Philebus calls pleasure a goddess at 12b. θεὸν τὴν ἡδονήν rendered 'a goddess' following the Philebus context. 'Maker' capitalised where it names God.
'half-brother of Hermes by the same father' (redundant) -> 'brother of Hermes on his father's side' (ὁμοπάτριος)
